arc: Five foundational sayings — names of the great divine persons and the law of their operation — are taught as the doctrinal ground upon which the Mind of Light is established in the soul, ending in the recognition that all the named realities form one living body until the last time.
reading:
This chapter belongs to the teaching of doctrinal foundations. The opening sentence names the matter exactly: "these five sayings which they utter make a foundation for the Mind of Light." What follows is therefore not narrative but catechesis. Five utterances — five names of divine persons and of the law of their working — are being set down as the discrete supports on which the awakened spiritual mind has to stand. In correspondence, a saying that "founds" the Mind of Light is a confirmed truth received and held in the rational; the five sayings are the five seals by which the regenerate mind is fixed against the mingled state. Their fivefold structure is the standard fullness of the natural-rational interface: the Mind of Light, when formed in a human, must be supported at all five degrees of reception.

The first saying names the Father. He is identified by what cannot be said of him: "the unnameable, who has no [name]," and yet within this very saying the Father is present. This is the lexicon's Father of Greatness — the inmost Divine Esse, source of all influx, who is reached not by description but by being invoked under the only name that confesses his unnameability. So the foundation of the Mind of Light begins where every spiritual mind must begin: with the acknowledgement of an inmost from which everything else proceeds, and which the rational does not contain.

The second saying turns from the hidden source to its sending-forth. It names the Ambassador and, in the same breath, "the [Father] of Life — whom they themselves call 'the Father of [Life]' — the First Father." Here the Father of Greatness is being read again under his operative aspect: the Living Spirit and the Third Ambassador, the awakening Call by which the hidden Father becomes a revealing image in the cosmos. The first saying confesses the Father in himself; the second confesses him as he sends forth. Together they establish what later tradition would call the inmost and the proceeding — the celestial source and its emanation toward the receptive.

The third saying is the Law: "the living law of those who are good and those who are bitter." This is the principle of discrimination — the sweetness and bitterness of the lexicon, the divine truth applied as judgment. Once the Father and his sending-forth are confessed, what must next be founded in the soul is the recognition that there is a law running through all things which divides the good from the corrupt taste, the regenerate state from the mingled. Without this third saying the Mind of Light could not be a discriminating mind; it would receive influx but not separate forth.

The fourth saying introduces the feminine subject who acts: "she gave the king of the aeons of light unto the Enmity; she humbled the [archons] and their cosmos; she poured upon them there in the boundary, until the last time." This is Divine Wisdom in her bringing-forth — the Mother of Life — read in her redemptive operation. She is the matrix through whom the First Man (the king of the aeons of light) is given over into Enmity, the cosmic principle of opposition, in order that the powers and their cosmos may be humbled and held under influx in the great middle-place between the two lands until the consummation. The saying founds in the regenerate mind the doctrine of the Lord's redemptive descent: that the king of the aeons was sent into the realm of self-love by the Wisdom-pole of the Divine, and that the present cosmos is precisely the boundary-state in which that self-giving is still operative.

The fifth saying gathers the rest into one: by "might… the cosmos stands firm," and "all of them, they are one body, living, beyond one another." This is the teaching that the Father, the Ambassador, the living Law, and the Mother's redemptive descent are not four separate doctrines but the articulation of one Grand Man — one living body whose members exceed one another in their discrete degrees yet hold together as a single form of love and wisdom in ultimates. The cosmos itself, far from being the King of Darkness's domain only, is being read here as the standing-firm of this one living body for as long as the boundary-time lasts. The fifth saying is therefore the saying of conjunction: it ties the previous four into the unity that the Mind of Light is meant finally to perceive.

So the spiritual process taught is the building of the rational foundation under the regenerate mind. First the inmost is confessed; then its sending-forth; then the law of discrimination by which good is sorted from bitter; then the redemptive descent of the king of light through the Mother into Enmity; and finally the recognition that all four, together with the cosmos held in the boundary, are one living body. To utter these five sayings is to set the five storehouses of received truth in order, so that the Mind of Light has somewhere to stand. Without them, the awakening of spiritual intelligence has no support; with them, the soul's understanding is grounded in the whole arc of the divine economy from the unnameable Father to the last time.

The lacunae are heavy in the central sections, but the surviving frame — five sayings, foundation, Father, Ambassador, Father of Life, First Father, the living law of good and bitter, the Mother giving the king of light into Enmity, the boundary, the last time, one living body — is enough to read the teaching as a single confessional foundation-laying for the awakened mind.
